grammar.title: Choosing between gerunds and infinitives
grammar.explanation:
A gerund is **verb + ing**. It looks like a verb, but it works like a noun in the sentence.

Use the gerund **after some verbs**. The most important ones are enjoy, like, love, hate, finish, stop, keep, and mind. When the teacher gives homework, the student must finish doing it before the next lesson.

Also use the gerund **after prepositions** like at, of, about, for, and in. Many students are good at reading, and their teacher is happy.

An infinitive is **to + verb**. Use it **after adjectives** like easy, hard, good, and nice. Every lesson feels easy when the student listens well.

Use the infinitive **after some verbs** too, like want, need, learn, decide, hope, and try. Every student wants to pass the exam on Friday.

Some verbs take **both forms** with the same meaning: start, begin, and continue. But be careful: try to do means make an effort, and try doing means see if you like it.
examples: The student *enjoys reading* English stories. (gerund after enjoy)
Our teacher is good *at explaining* every lesson. (gerund after the preposition at)
I *finished doing* my homework at six o'clock. (gerund after finish)
This lesson is easy *to understand*. (infinitive after the adjective easy)
She *wants to pass* the exam. (infinitive after want)
He *decided to study* with his teacher. (infinitive after decide)

practice.q: Which is correct: 'I enjoy to read' or 'I enjoy reading'?
practice.a: 'I enjoy reading'. Use the gerund after enjoy.

practice.q: Which is correct: 'I want pass the exam' or 'I want to pass the exam'?
practice.a: 'I want to pass the exam'. Use to + verb after want.
